Learn more × License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2608.00008v1 [cs.AI] 12 Jun 2026 Energy Efficiency of Locally Deployed LLMs: A Preliminary Quantitative GPU Power Benchmark on Consumer Hardware Philipp M. Zähl Affiliation: Institute for Digitalization Aachen FH Aachen University of Applied Sciences Aachen, Germany zaehl@fh-aachen.de Anika Hennig Affiliation: Institute for Digitalization Aachen FH Aachen University of Applied Sciences Aachen, Germany hennig@fh-aachen.de Abstract The local deployment of large language models (LLMs) is gaining traction due to privacy concerns and the desire for on-premise inference. However, the energy costs on consumer hardware remain poorly characterized, as most benchmarks focus solely on accuracy. This paper presents a reproducible, hardware-level energy benchmark of nine open-source LLMs (1B to 7B parameters) executed on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4060 Ti 16GB). Using the Ollama inference engine, GPU power draw was sampled at 2 Hz 2\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} via nvidia-smi across a fixed prompt set. We evaluate mean/peak power, total energy per prompt (J/prompt), energy per output token (J/token), and throughput (tok/s). Our findings suggest that factors beyond raw parameter count, including model architecture and quantization strategy, drive energy efficiency. Specifically, gemma3:1b and llama3.2:1b achieve the lowest energy cost ( 0.56 J − 1 0.56\text{\,}\mathrm{J}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1} and 0.65 J − 1 0.65\text{\,}\mathrm{J}\text{\,}{\mathrm{}}^{-1} ) and the highest throughput ( > > 170 tok / s 170\text{\,}\mathrm{t}\mathrm{o}\mathrm{k}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s} ). In contrast, the 7B-Mistral model consumes up to 4.4 × 4.4\times more energy per token than the most efficient model. Notably, qwen3.5:2b exhibits anomalously high per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning, highlighting the need to distinguish between token generation modes in efficiency metrics. Index Terms: benchmarking, energy efficiency, GPU power measurement, green AI, large language models, on-premise I Introduction The democratization of large language model inference through tools such as Ollama [ 1 ] , llama.cpp [ 2 ] , and LM Studio [ 3 ] has made it feasible for individual users and small organizations to run state-of-the-art language models locally, without transmitting data to third-party cloud providers [ 4 ] . Locally deployed models offer advantages in latency, data privacy, and long-term costs, but they also impose a continuous energy burden on the host machine that, at scale, is non-trivial [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . The environmental impact of large-scale AI training has been well documented [ 8 , 6 ] , but inference energy, especially on consumer hardware, is significantly less studied. For an end user running a 7B-parameter model as a daily assistant, the cumulative energy cost over months of use can rival that of other household appliances [ 5 , 6 , 9 ] . As model proliferation accelerates and edge-deployment tooling matures, understanding the energy-performance tradeoffs of available models becomes a practical engineering concern. This paper addresses the following research question: Among openly available language models deployable on a single consumer GPU, which models provide the most favorable energy efficiency, and how do efficiency metrics relate to model size and architecture ? Therefore, our contributions are fourfold: First, we provide a reproducible, open-source benchmark harness that instruments GPU power draw via nvidia-smi for containerized LLM inference workloads. Second, we contribute a diverse empirical baseline covering multiple energy and performance metrics across several open-source model families. Third, we provide a systematic analysis of the relationship between model size and energy efficiency, demonstrating how architectural scaling choices affect throughput and operational costs even when accounting for response quality. Finally, we offer new insights into how advanced prompting and reasoning mechanisms, such as extended chain-of-thought (CoT), fundamentally alter the established energy profiles of smaller model classes. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: First, Section II reviews related work. Then, Section III describes the experimental setup and measurement protocol. Section IV presents results, followed by a discussion on the implications in Section V . Finally, we conclude the paper in Section VI . II Related Work II-A Energy Cost of AI Workloads Strubell et al. [ 8 ] first brought attention to the substantial carbon footprint of training large natural language processing (NLP) models, reporting that training a single Transformer-based NLP model could emit as much CO 2 as five transatlantic flights. Patterson et al. [ 6 ] extended this analysis to include inference and found that, in production deployments, inference energy often dominates lifetime energy costs. Schwartz et al. [ 10 ] coined the term “Green AI” and called for efficiency metrics to be reported alongside accuracy in research publications. Argerich and Patiño-Martínez [ 5 ] reinforced this shift by arguing that since models are trained once but queried millions of times in production, the cumulative inference footprint quickly surpasses training costs, as demonstrated by the massive daily energy demands of real-world conversational agents. II-B LLM Inference Benchmarking Several recent efforts have benchmarked LLM inference performance. Aminabadi et al. [ 4 ] characterized the throughput and latency of large models under different parallelism strategies on server-class hardware. Frantar et al. [ 11 ] and Dettmers et al. [ 12 ] demonstrated that quantization dramatically reduces VRAM requirements and can improve inference speed, though its energy implications have not been systematically quantified for consumer deployments. Poddar et al. [ 7 ] addressed this gap through an extensive benchmarking of both encoder-decoder and decoder-only architectures across diverse NLP tasks, establishing that inference energy is more strongly correlated with output token length and response time than input characteristics. To further capture query-level variability, Maliakel et al. [ 13 ] demonstrated that surface-level heuristics like input length fail to predict computational difficulty, which is instead better explained by lightweight semantic features such as entity density. II-C Measurement Methodology Bannour et al. [ 14 ] surveyed tools for measuring the carbon footprint of NLP pipelines, including codecarbon [ 15 ] and Intel RAPL-based utilities. GPU-level measurement via nvidia-smi has been widely adopted in practice due to its availability on all NVIDIA-based systems, though prior work has noted a polling granularity limitation [ 16 ] . To overcome the challenge of profiling isolated hardware components, Argerich and Patiño-Martínez [ 5 ] introduced a pure software framework capable of granularly isolating CPU, memory, GPU, and storage energy draw on Linux systems. At the micro-architectural phase level, Maliakel et al. [ 13 ] leveraged NVML telemetry to separate the compute-bound prefill phase from the memory-bound autoregressive decode phase. They discovered that the decode phase dominates up to 91% of inference time but is highly insensitive to GPU core frequency, meaning that phase-aware dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) can yield up to 42% energy savings with negligible latency penalties. III Methodology III-A Testbed Hardware and Software All experiments were conducted on a single workstation running Ubuntu 24 under Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL2). Table I summarizes the hardware configuration. The host GPU, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Ti with 16 GiB 16\text{\,}\mathrm{GiB} GDDR6X VRAM and CUDA Compute Capability 8.9, was used exclusively for inference; no concurrent GPU workloads were active during measurement. TABLE I: Experimental Hardware Configuration Component Specification GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Ti VRAM 16 GiB 16\text{\,}\mathrm{GiB} GDDR6X GPU Compute Cap. 8.9 (Ada Lovelace) GPU Driver 591.86 CPU Intel i7-12700K (Cores: 10/20) Subsystem RAM 15.49 GiB 15.49\text{\,}\mathrm{GiB} ( 32 GiB 32\text{\,}\mathrm{GiB} available) Subsystem OS Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (WSL2, Windows 11) Inference Engine Ollama (Docker v4.69.0, GPU passthrough) Models were served by Ollama running inside an official Docker container ( ollama/ollama ) with full GPU passthrough ( --gpus all ). The Ollama API was accessed via HTTP at localhost:11434 using the /api/generate endpoint in non-streaming mode. III-B Models Under Test Nine openly available language models were selected to span a range of parameter sizes (1B-7B), model families, and quantization levels representative of the current Ollama model library. The main constraint in selecting a model was memory requirements: preference was given to models or model variants that require 8 GiB 8\text{\,}\mathrm{GiB} or less of memory. Table II lists the evaluated models. All models were obtained via ollama pull and use the default quantization shipped by the respective Ollama registry entry (typically 4-bit or 8-bit GGUF/AWQ quantization). TABLE II: Architectural and Operational Properties of Evaluated Models Model Tag Family Params Primary Type Context gemma3:1b Google Gemma 3 ∼ \sim 1B Multimodal / General 128k gemma3:4b Google Gemma 3 ∼ \sim 4B Multimodal / General 128k gemma4:e2b Google Gemma 4 ∼ \sim 2B Reasoning / Edge 128k llama3.2:1b Meta Llama 3.2 ∼ \sim 1B General / Edge 128k llama3.2:3b Meta Llama 3.2 ∼ \sim 3B General / Edge 128k mistral:7b Mistral ∼ \sim 7B General 32k phi4-mini:3.8b Microsoft Phi-4 ∼ \sim 3.8B Reasoning 128k qwen2.5:3b Alibaba Qwen 2.5 ∼ \sim 3B General 128k qwen3.5:2b Alibaba Qwen 3.5 ∼ \sim 2B Reasoning / Vision 262k III-C Prompt Set and Execution Protocol A fixed set of 15 prompts was designed to span a representative range of real-world inference workloads, deliberately varying expected output length and computational demand. The prompts were organized into three tiers: • Tier 1 - Short factual (5 prompts): Single-sentence questions with brief, deterministic answers (e.g., “What is the capital of France?” , “What is 17 multiplied by 23?” ). Expected output: 1-3 sentences. • Tier 2 - Medium reasoning (5 prompts): Questions requiring explanation or multi-step synthesis (e.g., “Explain the difference between TCP and UDP in two sentences.” , “What is gradient descent and why is it used in machine learning?” ). Expected output: 2-5 sentences. • Tier 3 - Long generation (5 prompts): Open-ended generation tasks demanding structured, multi-paragraph responses (e.g., “Write a Python function that checks whether a given string is a palindrome. Include docstring and tests.” , “Explain how a transformer neural network works. Cover attention mechanisms, tokenisation, and training.” ). Expected output: 15-30 sentences. This tiered design ensures that aggregate statistics are not dominated by either trivially short or unusually long completions and mirrors the heterogeneous workloads encountered in practice. The complete prompt file is included in the appendix. Each model processed the full 15-prompt set in three independent runs, yielding 15 × 3 = 45 15\times 3=45 prompt-level observations per model ( 405 405 total). Three repetitions were selected as a pragmatic trade-off between experimental runtime and measurement robustness. Although some run-to-run variability was observed, it remained modest and did not alter the relative ranking or overall trends across models, indicating that three repetitions were sufficient for reliable comparative analysis. Title: Researchers Develop Novel Approach for Machine Learning Adapter Merging

In the realm of machine learning, a team of researchers has proposed a novel method for merging machine learning adapters, a development that could potentially streamline the integration of various models in complex systems.

The research, titled "LoRA: A Machine Learning Adapter Merging Framework," was published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research. The paper outlines a framework called LoRA, which stands for "Learned Representation of Adapters."

LoRA is designed to address the challenges associated with merging multiple machine learning adapters, a process that can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. The framework aims to simplify this process by learning a compact and efficient representation of the adapters, thereby facilitating their integration.

The researchers claim that LoRA can significantly reduce the computational cost and memory requirements associated with merging machine learning adapters. However, the paper does not provide specific details about the performance of the framework or the complexity of the systems it can handle.

The development of LoRA could have significant implications for industries that rely heavily on machine learning, such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, and artificial intelligence. By simplifying the process of merging machine learning adapters, LoRA could potentially lead to more efficient and effective systems.

However, it is important to note that the research is still in its early stages. The paper does not provide any test results or real-world applications of the framework. Furthermore, the long-term impact of LoRA on the field of machine learning is still uncertain.

In conclusion, the research presents a novel approach for merging machine learning adapters, a development that could potentially streamline the integration of various models in complex systems. While the paper does not provide specific details about the performance of the framework, it could have significant implications for industries that rely heavily on machine learning. The long-term impact of LoRA on the field of machine learning remains to be seen.
